claim: The study was conducted longitudinally over 10 years in a sample of 126 subjects aged 8-33 years.
source: We present results from a longitudinal study conducted over 10 years in a sample of 126 8–33 year olds
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract and confirmed in methods section describing 152 subjects tested with 126 meeting inclusion criteria.

claim: Adolescent development of working memory is supported by decreased variability in the amplitude of expression of whole brain states of task-related activity.
source: We present results from a longitudinal study conducted over 10 years in a sample of 126 8–33 year olds demonstrating that adolescent development of working memory is supported by decreased variability in the amplitude of expression of whole brain states of task-related activity.
evidence: Main finding stated in abstract and supported by fMRI data showing brain state variability decreases with age.

claim: Putative gain signals affecting maintenance and retrieval aspects of working memory processing stabilize during adolescence.
source: fMRI analyses reveal that putative gain signals affecting maintenance and retrieval aspects of working memory processing stabilize during adolescence, while those affecting sensorimotor processes do not.
evidence: Supported by analysis showing maintenance- and retrieval-related brain state variability decreases with age while VME-related variability does not.

claim: Gain signals affecting sensorimotor processes do not stabilize during adolescence.
source: fMRI analyses reveal that putative gain signals affecting maintenance and retrieval aspects of working memory processing stabilize during adolescence, while those affecting sensorimotor processes do not.
evidence: Supported by finding that VME-related brain state variability did not significantly decrease with age.

claim: Trial-to-trial variability in reaction time of eye-movements during a memory guided saccade task is related to fluctuations in the amplitude of expression of task-related brain states.
source: We show that trial-to-trial variability in the reaction time and accuracy of eye-movements during a memory guided saccade task are related to fluctuations in the amplitude of expression of task-related brain states, or brain state variability
evidence: Demonstrated through regression analyses showing brain state expression at specific TRs predicts trial-wise RT.

claim: Trial-to-trial variability in accuracy of eye-movements during a memory guided saccade task is related to fluctuations in the amplitude of expression of task-related brain states.
source: We show that trial-to-trial variability in the reaction time and accuracy of eye-movements during a memory guided saccade task are related to fluctuations in the amplitude of expression of task-related brain states, or brain state variability
evidence: Demonstrated through regression analyses showing brain state expression predicts trial-wise saccadic error.

claim: Individual developmental trajectories of reaction time variability are related to individual trajectories of brain state variability.
source: and also provide evidence that individual developmental trajectories of reaction time variability are related to individual trajectories of brain state variability.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis in 29 subjects with 4+ sessions showing r=-0.48, p=0.008.

claim: The stabilization of widespread gain signals affecting already available cognitive processes underlies the maturation of cognition during adolescence.
source: These observations demonstrate that the stabilization of widespread gain signals affecting already available cognitive processes underlies the maturation of cognition during adolescence.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the combined findings of decreased brain state variability and its relationship to behavioral stabilization.

claim: Core working memory processes are available as early as infancy.
source: Working memory (WM), the ability to retain information online in order to guide goal directed behavior, is evident in rudimentary form as early as infancy (Diamond and Goldman-Rakic, 1989; Gilmore and Johnson, 1995), indicating that core WM processes are available throughout development.
evidence: Supported by citations to Diamond and Goldman-Rakic, 1989 and Gilmore and Johnson, 1995.

claim: Working memory continues to develop across adolescence and into early adulthood.
source: However, protracted improvements in performance, typically measured as the percentage of correctly performed trials or as changes in mean behavioral response metrics, such as reaction time and accuracy, demonstrate that WM continues to develop across adolescence and into early adulthood (Gathercole et al., 2004; Luna et al., 2004; Alloway et al., 2006; Crone et al., 2006; Thomason et al., 2009; Luna et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations documenting developmental improvements in WM performance.

claim: Developmental decreases in behavioral variability during cognitive tasks are evident through adolescence.
source: Developmental decreases in behavioral variability during cognitive tasks are also evident through adolescence (McIntosh et al., 2008; Klein et al., 2011; Tamnes et al., 2012), however this has not been directly examined in the context of WM.
evidence: Supported by citations to McIntosh et al., 2008; Klein et al., 2011; Tamnes et al., 2012.

claim: Behavioral variability during cognitive tasks has not been directly examined in the context of working memory prior to this study.
source: Developmental decreases in behavioral variability during cognitive tasks are also evident through adolescence (McIntosh et al., 2008; Klein et al., 2011; Tamnes et al., 2012), however this has not been directly examined in the context of WM.
evidence: Statement of gap in literature that this study addresses.

claim: Excessive behavioral variability frequently attends disorders such as schizophrenia.
source: Behavioral variability, or intra-individual variability, is a sensitive barometer of cognitive function; excessive variability frequently attends disorders such as schizophrenia (Kaiser et al., 2008); ADHD (Munoz et al., 2003); and age-related cognitive decline (MacDonald et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kaiser et al., 2008.

claim: Excessive behavioral variability frequently attends ADHD.
source: Behavioral variability, or intra-individual variability, is a sensitive barometer of cognitive function; excessive variability frequently attends disorders such as schizophrenia (Kaiser et al., 2008); ADHD (Munoz et al., 2003); and age-related cognitive decline (MacDonald et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Munoz et al., 2003.

claim: Excessive behavioral variability frequently attends age-related cognitive decline.
source: Behavioral variability, or intra-individual variability, is a sensitive barometer of cognitive function; excessive variability frequently attends disorders such as schizophrenia (Kaiser et al., 2008); ADHD (Munoz et al., 2003); and age-related cognitive decline (MacDonald et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to MacDonald et al., 2006.

claim: Behavioral variability has been found to be associated with fluctuations in neural signals occurring within individual brain areas.
source: Behavioral variability has been found to be associated with fluctuations in neural (Newsome et al., 1989; Cohen et al., 2009; Nienborg and Cumming, 2009) or blood-oxygen-level dependent (BOLD) signals occurring within individual brain areas (Wagner et al., 1998; Ress and Heeger, 2003; Yarkoni et al., 2009), and networks of brain areas (Rosenberg et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations documenting brain-behavior relationships.

claim: Behavioral variability has been found to be associated with fluctuations in BOLD signals occurring within individual brain areas.
source: Behavioral variability has been found to be associated with fluctuations in neural (Newsome et al., 1989; Cohen et al., 2009; Nienborg and Cumming, 2009) or blood-oxygen-level dependent (BOLD) signals occurring within individual brain areas (Wagner et al., 1998; Ress and Heeger, 2003; Yarkoni et al., 2009), and networks of brain areas (Rosenberg et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wagner et al., 1998; Ress and Heeger, 2003; Yarkoni et al., 2009.

claim: Behavioral variability has been found to be associated with fluctuations in signals occurring within networks of brain areas.
source: Behavioral variability has been found to be associated with fluctuations in neural (Newsome et al., 1989; Cohen et al., 2009; Nienborg and Cumming, 2009) or blood-oxygen-level dependent (BOLD) signals occurring within individual brain areas (Wagner et al., 1998; Ress and Heeger, 2003; Yarkoni et al., 2009), and networks of brain areas (Rosenberg et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rosenberg et al., 2016.

claim: Brain/behavior relationships are driven, at least in part, by trial-to-trial variability in gain modulating signals.
source: Several lines of research suggest that these brain/behavior relationships are driven, at least in part, by trial-to-trial variability in gain modulating signals (Fox et al., 2006; Eldar et al., 2013; Rabinowitz et al., 2015) that enhance the activity of individual neurons or brain areas experiencing net excitation and further suppress the activity of neurons or areas experiencing net inhibition (Servan-Schreiber et al., 1990).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fox et al., 2006; Eldar et al., 2013; Rabinowitz et al., 2015.

claim: Gain modulating signals enhance the activity of individual neurons or brain areas experiencing net excitation and further suppress the activity of neurons or areas experiencing net inhibition.
source: Several lines of research suggest that these brain/behavior relationships are driven, at least in part, by trial-to-trial variability in gain modulating signals (Fox et al., 2006; Eldar et al., 2013; Rabinowitz et al., 2015) that enhance the activity of individual neurons or brain areas experiencing net excitation and further suppress the activity of neurons or areas experiencing net inhibition (Servan-Schreiber et al., 1990).
evidence: Supported by citation to Servan-Schreiber et al., 1990.

claim: Some gain modulating signals are shared across cortical areas.
source: Recent electrophysiological evidence indicates that some gain modulating signals are shared across cortical areas and that moment-to-moment variation in such distributed gain signaling may account for a significant portion of neural and behavioral variability (Rabinowitz et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rabinowitz et al., 2015.

claim: Moment-to-moment variation in distributed gain signaling may account for a significant portion of neural and behavioral variability.
source: Recent electrophysiological evidence indicates that some gain modulating signals are shared across cortical areas and that moment-to-moment variation in such distributed gain signaling may account for a significant portion of neural and behavioral variability (Rabinowitz et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rabinowitz et al., 2015.

claim: The structure of neural covariance within populations of simultaneously recorded sensory neurons is best explained as the result of multiple ongoing gain modulating signals.
source: Additionally, the structure of neural covariance within populations of simultaneously recorded sensory neurons is best explained as the result of multiple ongoing gain modulating signals (Rabinowitz et al., 2015), raising the possibility that different sources of gain variability affect neural activity in a functionally targeted way.
evidence: Supported by citation to Rabinowitz et al., 2015.

claim: Different sources of gain variability may affect neural activity in a functionally targeted way.
source: Additionally, the structure of neural covariance within populations of simultaneously recorded sensory neurons is best explained as the result of multiple ongoing gain modulating signals (Rabinowitz et al., 2015), raising the possibility that different sources of gain variability affect neural activity in a functionally targeted way.
evidence: Inference drawn from the cited finding about multiple gain signals.

claim: Widespread or global gain modulating processes would not change the spatial distribution or 'pattern' of task evoked neural activity.
source: Widespread or global gain modulating processes would not, by definition, change the spatial distribution or 'pattern' of task evoked neural activity.
evidence: Theoretical statement based on the definition of gain modulation.

claim: Global gain modulating processes would influence the amplitude with which task-evoked neural activity patterns are expressed.
source: Rather, they would influence the amplitude with which they are expressed, manifesting as trial-to-trial variability in the amplitude of expression of whole-brain patterns of activity that support task-relevant processes.
evidence: Theoretical prediction based on the definition of gain modulation.

claim: Average reaction time decreases during development following an age^-1 trajectory.
source: Using a linear mixed-effects model to account for the longitudinal nature of the data, we found, consistent with prior findings (Luna et al., 2004), that average RT and inaccuracy decreases during development following an age−1 trajectory (Figure 1c,e).
evidence: Demonstrated through linear mixed-effects modeling of longitudinal data, shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Saccade inaccuracy decreases during development following an age^-1 trajectory.
source: Using a linear mixed-effects model to account for the longitudinal nature of the data, we found, consistent with prior findings (Luna et al., 2004), that average RT and inaccuracy decreases during development following an age−1 trajectory (Figure 1c,e).
evidence: Demonstrated through linear mixed-effects modeling of longitudinal data, shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Average reaction time decreased by approximately 239 ms (39% decline) between ages 8 and 33.
source: We estimated how much each behavioral measure changed at the group level between the ages of 8 and 33 and observed a reduction in average RT amounting to approximately 239 ms, a 39% decline (t(1346)=9.30; p=6.03e-20
evidence: Quantitative result from statistical analysis of developmental trajectory.

claim: Inaccuracy decreased by approximately 0.25° (47% decline) between ages 8 and 33.
source: Inaccuracy decreased by approximately 0.25°, or 47% (t(1346)=3.11; p=0.0019).
evidence: Quantitative result from statistical analysis of developmental trajectory.

claim: The standard deviation of reaction time decreases with development following an age^-1 trajectory.
source: Importantly, both measures of behavioral variability also decrease with development following an age−1 trajectory (Figure 1d,f).
evidence: Demonstrated through linear mixed-effects modeling, shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The imprecision of memory-guided saccades decreases with development following an age^-1 trajectory.
source: Importantly, both measures of behavioral variability also decrease with development following an age−1 trajectory (Figure 1d,f).
evidence: Demonstrated through linear mixed-effects modeling, shown in Figure 1f.

claim: The developmental change in the standard deviation of RT amounts to approximately 156 ms, a 67% reduction.
source: The developmental change in the standard deviation of RT amounts to approximately 156 ms, a 67% reduction (t(1346)=7.84; p=9.4e-15).
evidence: Quantitative result from statistical analysis of developmental trajectory.

claim: The imprecision of the MGS decreases with age by approximately 0.87° of visual angle, a 35% change.
source: The imprecision of the MGS decreases with age, resulting in an estimated reduction of 0.87° of visual angle, a change, which amounts to roughly 35% (t(1346)=4.03; p=5.83e-5).
evidence: Quantitative result from statistical analysis of developmental trajectory.

claim: A model predicting age from mean RT was significantly improved by including the standard deviation of RT.
source: We found that a null model predicting age from only mean RT was significantly improved by including the standard deviation of RT (null model: DF=4 AIC=−2212.7, Log-Likelihood=1110.4; full model: DF=5 AIC=−2220.7, Log-Likelihood=1115.6; p=0.002)(Burnham and Anderson, 2004).
evidence: Result from model comparison analysis showing RT variability provides unique information about developmental status.

claim: Including imprecision as a term improved model performance predicting age from inaccuracy, but the difference did not achieve statistical significance.
source: Including imprecision as a term improved model performance, but the difference did not achieve statistical significance (null model: DF=4, AIC=−2108.4, Log-Likelihood=1058.2; full model: DF=5 AIC=−2110.1, Log-Likelihood=1060.0, p=0.052).
evidence: Result from model comparison analysis.

claim: Reaction time variability, but not imprecision, appears to measurably reflect a unique aspect of cognitive development.
source: Thus, of the two measures of behavioral variability, reaction time variability, but not imprecision, appears to measurably reflect a unique aspect of cognitive development.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from model comparison results.

claim: Minimal age-related differences were observed in the average time courses of brain state expression.
source: To determine whether such differences were present, we performed omnibus F-tests on the brain state time courses for each task condition to assess the null hypotheses that all of the coefficients for Age*TR (Age*TR*TargetHemifield in the case of the spatial brain state components) were equal to zero. We observed minimal age-related differences in the average time courses of brain state expression.
evidence: Result from omnibus F-tests on brain state time courses.

claim: Age-related differences were observed for the spatial, but not mean, component of the VME states across all trial types.
source: These differences were observed for the spatial, but not mean, component of the VME states across all trial types (all p<0.001).
evidence: Result from omnibus F-tests.

claim: No significant age-related differences were detected in the expression of either mean or spatial components of the maintenance state.
source: We did not detect any significant age-related differences in the expression of either mean or spatial components of the maintenance state (all p>0.14).
evidence: Result from omnibus F-tests.

claim: The peak amplitude of spatial VME expression did not differ significantly with age.
source: We therefore examined the Age*Target interaction term, which we found did not reach significance (t(2696)=1.59; p=0.111).
evidence: Result from statistical test of peak amplitude differences.

claim: Mean global gain does not change during adolescent development.
source: Even here, however, the age-related differences were not ones of amplitude, but of duration, suggesting that mean global gain does not change during adolescent development.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from analyses showing minimal age-related differences in amplitude of brain state expression.

claim: Trials with faster RTs were associated with greater early expression of the mean VME and maintenance brain states (TRs 0–2).
source: Trials with faster RTs were associated with greater early expression of the mean VME and maintenance brain states (TRs 0–2), and reduced later expression of all mean states (TRs 3–5).
evidence: Result from regression analyses relating brain state expression to trial-wise RT.

claim: Trials with faster RTs were associated with reduced later expression of all mean states (TRs 3–5).
source: Trials with faster RTs were associated with greater early expression of the mean VME and maintenance brain states (TRs 0–2), and reduced later expression of all mean states (TRs 3–5).
evidence: Result from regression analyses relating brain state expression to trial-wise RT.

claim: Greater saccadic error was associated with greater expression of the mean VME state (TR 3).
source: Greater SE was associated with greater expression of the mean VME state (TR 3).
evidence: Result from regression analyses relating brain state expression to trial-wise saccadic error.

claim: The fastest RTs occurred when whole-brain patterns of task-related activity were biased in the direction of the target.
source: The fastest RTs occurred when whole-brain patterns of task-related activity were biased in the direction of the target (VME: TRs 1–3; maintenance and retrieval: TRs 1–2).
evidence: Result from analyses of spatial brain state components and their relationship to RT.

claim: Greater target hemifield appropriate expression of the spatial VME state (TRs 2–3) was associated with increased saccadic error.
source: Interestingly, greater target hemifield appropriate expression of the spatial VME state (TRs 2–3) was associated with increased SE, indicating that increasing the amplitude of its expression does not improve all aspects of task performance.
evidence: Result from regression analyses showing relationship between spatial VME state and saccadic error.

claim: Increased hemifield appropriate expression of the spatial component of the maintenance states (TR 3) was associated with reduced saccadic error.
source: Increased hemifield appropriate expression of the spatial component of the maintenance states (TR 3), in contrast, was associated with reduced SE.
evidence: Result from regression analyses showing relationship between spatial maintenance state and saccadic error.

claim: A significant quadratic relationship exists between z-scored RT and SE at the trial level.
source: We found a significant quadratic relationship between z-scored RT and SE at the trial level indicating that, within a session, excessively fast and slow responses were associated with reduced accuracy (t(16754)=4.64; p=3.52e-6).
evidence: Result from statistical analysis examining speed-accuracy trade-off.

claim: Within a session, excessively fast and slow responses were associated with reduced accuracy.
source: We found a significant quadratic relationship between z-scored RT and SE at the trial level indicating that, within a session, excessively fast and slow responses were associated with reduced accuracy (t(16754)=4.64; p=3.52e-6).
evidence: Result from statistical analysis showing speed-accuracy trade-off.

claim: The trial-wise relationship between RT and the expression of the mean VME brain state reflects a mixture of both time-shifted BOLD response and a true relationship between gain fluctuation and performance.
source: We found that the trial-wise relationship between RT and the expression of the mean VME brain state —the state associated with eye-movements— was inconsistent with both a purely amplitude-based mechanism, and purely timing-based mechanism and instead is likely to reflect a mixture of both the trivial time shifted BOLD response, and a true relationship between gain fluctuation and performance (Figure 5, column 4).
evidence: Result from simulation analyses comparing different mechanisms, shown in Figure 5.

claim: Total brain state variability decreases with age after controlling for mean frame-wise displacement and the number of correctly performed trials.
source: We found that total brain state variability decreases with age (Figure 6a) after controlling for mean frame-wise displacement (FD)(Power et al., 2012; Siegel et al., 2014) and the number of correctly performed trials (t(333)=-3.35; p=9.0e-4).
evidence: Result from regression analysis controlling for confounds, shown in Figure 6a.

claim: The proportion of VME-related brain state variability did not significantly decrease with age.
source: The proportion of VME-related brain state variability did not significantly decrease with age (t(333)=-1.47; p=0.14).
evidence: Result from statistical analysis of VME component of brain state variability.

claim: Maintenance-related brain state variability shows significant age-related decrease.
source: However, maintenance- and retrieval-related brain state variability both show significant age-related decreases (t(333)=-3.8; p=1.8e-4 and t(333)=-5.53; p=6.27e-8 respectively).
evidence: Result from statistical analysis of maintenance component of brain state variability.

claim: Retrieval-related brain state variability shows significant age-related decrease.
source: However, maintenance- and retrieval-related brain state variability both show significant age-related decreases (t(333)=-3.8; p=1.8e-4 and t(333)=-5.53; p=6.27e-8 respectively).
evidence: Result from statistical analysis of retrieval component of brain state variability.

claim: Trajectories of VME and retrieval-related variability cannot be significantly distinguished from one another.
source: Pairwise comparisons of slopes reveal that trajectories of VME and retrieval-related variability can not be significantly distinguished from one another (t(670)=0.60; p=0.54)
evidence: Result from pairwise comparison of developmental trajectories.

claim: Maintenance-related brain state variability decreases more slowly through adolescence compared to both VME and retrieval-related variability.
source: while maintenance-related brain state variability decreases more slowly through adolescence compared to both VME and retrieval-related variability (t(670)= 2.44; p=0.014 and t(670)=-3.71; p=2.2e-4 respectively).
evidence: Result from pairwise comparisons of developmental trajectory slopes.

claim: Reversing the relationship between motion and age does not significantly alter the finding that older subjects exhibited less brain state variability than younger subjects.
source: We found that reversing the relationship between motion and age does not significantly alter our finding that older subjects exhibited less brain state variability than younger subjects (Figure 7).
evidence: Result from biased bootstrap analysis controlling for motion, shown in Figure 7.

claim: A negative correlation exists between individual brain state variability slopes and reaction time variability slopes (r = −0.48; p=0.008).
source: We observed just such a negative relationship for reaction time variability (r = −0.48; p=0.008) (Figure 8a).
evidence: Result from correlation analysis in subset of 29 subjects with 4+ sessions, shown in Figure 8a.

claim: The within-subject relationship between brain state variability and saccade imprecision was not significant in the subset of 29 subjects with 4+ sessions.
source: However, the within-subject relationship between brain state variability and saccade imprecision was not significant (r=0.28; p=0.14) (Figure 8b).
evidence: Result from correlation analysis in subset of 29 subjects, shown in Figure 8b.

claim: A significant positive relationship exists between total brain state variability and saccade imprecision in the entire sample.
source: Here we did observe a significant positive relationship between total brain state variability and saccade imprecision (t(1344)=3.2; p=0.001) (Figure 8c).
evidence: Result from analysis using entire sample with age as covariate, shown in Figure 8c.

claim: Core cognitive functions are online by childhood.
source: Our results, in sum, provide compelling evidence that core cognitive functions are online by childhood and what underlies cognitive development through adolescence is a fine-tuning of the ability to stabilize the expression neural activity associated with those cognitive processes.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the overall pattern of results showing stabilization rather than emergence of functions.

claim: What underlies cognitive development through adolescence is a fine-tuning of the ability to stabilize the expression of neural activity associated with cognitive processes.
source: Our results, in sum, provide compelling evidence that core cognitive functions are online by childhood and what underlies cognitive development through adolescence is a fine-tuning of the ability to stabilize the expression neural activity associated with those cognitive processes.
evidence: Main conclusion drawn from the combined findings of the study.

claim: Fluctuations in the activity of midbrain and brain stem nuclei affect resting state connectivity in a functionally organized way.
source: Recent fMRI studies have shown that fluctuations in the activity of midbrain and brain stem nuclei affect resting state connectivity in what appears to be a functionally organized way (Bär et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bär et al., 2016.

claim: Cholinergic modulation amplifies the spatially selective effects of perceptual processing and attention in a manner analogous to fluctuations in spatial brain state components.
source: Similarly, cholinergic modulation has been shown to amplify the spatially selective effects of perceptual processing and attention in a manner analogous to fluctuations in our spatial brain state components (Furey et al., 2000; Bentley et al., 2004; Rokem et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Furey et al., 2000; Bentley et al., 2004; Rokem et al., 2010.

claim: Myelination and synaptic pruning continue to progress in critical brain systems.
source: Finally, myelination and synaptic pruning, which continue to progress in critical brain systems (Simmonds et al., 2014), occurring at different rates for different brain regions, (Petanjek et al., 2011) may also affect neural signal to noise ratios and play a role in the stability of gain signals that contribute to behavioral variability.
evidence: Supported by citations to Simmonds et al., 2014 and Petanjek et al., 2011.

claim: Myelination and synaptic pruning occur at different rates for different brain regions.
source: Finally, myelination and synaptic pruning, which continue to progress in critical brain systems (Simmonds et al., 2014), occurring at different rates for different brain regions, (Petanjek et al., 2011) may also affect neural signal to noise ratios and play a role in the stability of gain signals that contribute to behavioral variability.
evidence: Supported by citation to Petanjek et al., 2011.

claim: Myelination and synaptic pruning may affect neural signal to noise ratios and play a role in the stability of gain signals that contribute to behavioral variability.
source: Finally, myelination and synaptic pruning, which continue to progress in critical brain systems (Simmonds et al., 2014), occurring at different rates for different brain regions, (Petanjek et al., 2011) may also affect neural signal to noise ratios and play a role in the stability of gain signals that contribute to behavioral variability.
evidence: Speculative statement about potential mechanisms.

claim: Brain state variability suggests that brain/behavior correlations like CP and DP should be widespread throughout task-related brain areas.
source: Brain state variability is consistent with this hypothesis and expands upon it in two ways 1) That brain state variability is the covariation of many task-related (and presumably behaviorally relevant) brain regions suggests that brain/behavior correlations like CP and DP should be wide-spread throughout task-related brain areas
evidence: Inference drawn from the concept of brain state variability.

claim: Fluctuations in multiple functionally specific global gain signals contribute to observed brain behavior correlations.
source: and 2) Our finding of distinct developmental trajectories of brain state variability affecting different task-related processes suggests that fluctuations in multiple functionally specific global gain signals contribute to observed brain behavior correlations.
evidence: Inference drawn from the finding of distinct developmental trajectories for different brain state components.

claim: Stable behavioral performance requires similarly stable allocation of top-down control processes, like attention.
source: An attractive model that would provide synthesis for our findings and those discussed above is that stable behavioral performance requires similarly stable allocation of top-down control processes, like attention.
evidence: Proposed theoretical model synthesizing the findings.

claim: Top-down processes partly exert their influence through multiple widespread gain signals that are functionally targeted, differentially affecting sensorimotor and cognitive processes.
source: Such top-down processes partly exert their influence through multiple widespread gain signals that are functionally targeted, differentially affecting sensorimotor and cognitive processes.
evidence: Part of proposed theoretical model.

claim: The stabilizing of working memory behavioral performance during adolescent development is the result of stabilizing gain signals that affect working memory maintenance and retrieval processes.
source: In this model, the stabilizing of working memory behavioral performance that we observed during adolescent development is the result of stabilizing those gain signals that affect working memory maintenance and retrieval processes.
evidence: Conclusion of the proposed theoretical model based on study findings.

claim: 152 subjects between the ages of 8 and 33 were tested.
source: We tested 152 subjects between the ages of 8 and 33.
evidence: Stated in methods section describing subject recruitment.

claim: Subjects were scanned approximately annually for 1–10 years.
source: Subjects were initially recruited between the ages of 8 and 30 years and were scanned approximately annually for 1–10 years.
evidence: Description of longitudinal study design in methods.

claim: After applying exclusion criteria, the dataset consisted of 126 subjects (60 female).
source: After applying these exclusion parameters our dataset consisted of 126 subjects (60 female).
evidence: Final sample size after exclusions stated in methods.

claim: Subjects with mean frame-wise displacement less than 0.15 mm were included.
source: Subjects were included based on two criteria: (1) Mean frame-wise displacement (FD) was less than 0.15 mm
evidence: Inclusion criterion stated in methods.

claim: Subjects with at least 50% of trials from each of the four trial types measurably correct were included.
source: and (2) at least 50% of the trials from each of the four trial types had to be measurably correct.
evidence: Inclusion criterion stated in methods.

claim: The study varied the duration of the initial target presentation (either 1.5 or 3 s).
source: We varied the duration of the initial target presentation (either 1.5 or 3 s) and the duration of the delay (1.5 or 9 s).
evidence: Task design parameter stated in introduction.

claim: The study varied the duration of the delay (1.5 or 9 s).
source: We varied the duration of the initial target presentation (either 1.5 or 3 s) and the duration of the delay (1.5 or 9 s).
evidence: Task design parameter stated in introduction.

claim: The target stimulus appeared at one of six locations: ±3, 6, or 9° along the horizontal visual meridian.
source: On each trial, subjects first made a visually guided 'encoding' saccade to the target stimulus, which appeared at one of six locations: ±3, 6, or 9° along the horizontal visual meridian, during an initial visuomotor/encoding (VME) epoch.
evidence: Task design parameter stated in introduction.

claim: Children typically have difficulty suppressing orienting saccades to target stimuli.
source: Children typically have difficulty suppressing orienting saccades to target stimuli (Luna et al., 2004)
evidence: Supported by citation to Luna et al., 2004.

claim: Allowing subjects to make the initial encoding saccade removed a possible age-related source of behavioral differences related to response inhibition rather than WM performance.
source: by allowing subjects to make the initial encoding saccade, we removed a possible age-related source of behavioral differences that would be related to response inhibition rather than WM performance.
evidence: Rationale for task design stated in introduction.

claim: Imaging data were acquired using a Siemens 3-Tesla MAGNETOM Allegra system.
source: Imaging data were acquired using a Siemens 3-Tesla MAGNETOM Allegra (Erlangen, Germany) system with a standard radio-frequency (RF) head coil at the Brain Imaging Research Center, University of Pittsburgh, Pittsburgh, PA.
evidence: MRI acquisition parameters stated in methods.

claim: Functional images were acquired using a gradient echo echo-planar (EPI) sequence with TR=1.5 s.
source: Functional images were acquired using a gradient echo echo-planar (EPI) sequence sensitive to blood-oxygen-dependent (BOLD) contrast (T2*) (TR=1.5 s, TE=25 ms, flip angle=70°, voxel size=3.125×3.125×4 mm slice resolution, 229 volumes).
evidence: MRI acquisition parameters stated in methods.

claim: Twenty-nine slices per volume were collected with no gap and aligned to the anterior and posterior commissure (AC-PC) plane.
source: Twenty-nine slices per volume were collected with no gap and aligned to the anterior and posterior commissure (AC-PC) plane.
evidence: MRI acquisition parameters stated in methods.
